title: Forest Shelters and Bunker Survival in Skala
summary: Accounts of bunker builders, hidden families, and survivors illuminate both the danger and resourcefulness of people seeking refuge near Skala.

## From hiding in town to the forest

For Skala’s Jews, the forest became a refuge after hiding in houses, basements, and attics grew increasingly dangerous. It was not a single, secure sanctuary. People moved between scattered shelters, depended on food obtained at risk, and faced discovery by German forces and local collaborators. The memorial book preserves both the practical knowledge behind their hiding places and the terrible consequences when those places were found.

The book’s account describes a group led by [Chaim Gatesfeld](/communities/skala/records/mention_a54c48f785c4a190e3433b70) and Nehemiah Stak. A survivor’s narrative says that their group built primitive forest shacks for shelter from rain and cold, as well as underground bunkers for emergencies. Bunkers accommodated roughly six to ten people. Hidden ventilation channels and small fireplaces made it possible to cook at night; branches, bushes, and leaves helped disguise the entrances. The group shifted locations every few weeks, wary that a settled routine—or smoke—could reveal them.

The book also records [Nehemiah Stak](/communities/skala/records/mention_aef975fea887996eae94bc00) and his sister [Malka Shtak](/communities/skala/records/mention_860ac74203720352b54c4a33), who had escaped from Borshchiv to Skala. They were among people whose survival depended not only on concealment but on movement, vigilance, and chance. A separate passage says that six named men began building new bunkers deep in the forest during winter, though the supplied record does not identify those builders individually. It would be misleading to assume this was exactly the same construction effort as the summer shelters.

The memorial book’s broader narrative gives a sense of the scale and diversity of this forest refuge: it recalls the colony growing to about 150 people by mid-August 1943, spread across different parts of the woods. A separate community record describes an underground colony of 28 people in winter 1943. These figures need not contradict one another: one describes a larger, dispersed population at a different moment, the other a particular counted group. The evidence does not establish that every forest survivor belonged to one organized colony.

## Hunger, exposure, and the fragile work of staying hidden

Concealment alone could not keep people alive. The forest’s cold, rain, and snow made shelter essential, but hunger repeatedly drove people out to seek food. The memorial book describes survivors going at night to nearby settlements to beg, barter, or buy provisions, and gathering what they could from fields and orchards. The account remembers help from some Polish peasants and from Ukrainian forester Radchuk and his wife; it also describes the risks of approaching anyone beyond the group.

Winter sharpened those risks. Snow could make movement harder and expose tracks; daytime smoke might be seen from afar. The book recalls people cooking only at night when winter conditions made travel dangerous. Its testimony also distinguishes between groups’ different practices: some survivors built bunkers, moved periodically, and took precautions about fires, while others—according to one narrator—stayed together in larger groups or relied on the belief that the forest was too vast for pursuers to search. The book presents that confidence as a fatal mistake, but it cannot tell us that every group faced the same conditions or made the same choices.

Within the underground colony, survival also meant sustaining one another emotionally. A survivor remembers winter nights in the bunker, lamplight, conversation, and Yiddish songs. Israel Fleischman’s singing brought back a song from a Skala amateur-theater production, whose final image of being “buried alive” resonated painfully with life underground. This is not a description of safety: it is a witness’s memory of how people tried to hold onto shared culture and feeling while living in concealment.

The names in the book make clear that families and individuals faced these dangers together. In the second bunker, it names [Moshe Dunaier](/communities/skala/records/mention_61f16622de2896ab8bcb0104), [Sarah Frankel](/communities/skala/records/mention_c5f409e933d1302e9aced70f), and [Frida Frankel](/communities/skala/records/mention_68a01a757bb2d661382d51bb), along with her daughters [Rita Frankel](/communities/skala/records/mention_4a701123d050cb9d964a7690) and [Mira Frankel](/communities/skala/records/mention_90b92c832a6e4b1a5a70cc10). The evidence identifies them as people hiding there; it does not establish every family member’s eventual fate. That distinction matters in a record shaped by testimony and loss.

## When bunkers were discovered

The book’s most harrowing accounts describe discovery as a sequence of coercion and violence. In one episode, Ukrainian militiamen located a bunker after capturing Max Bretschneider, whom the narrative says they beat and tortured until he led them to the hiding place. They fired into the bunker, then pushed in burning straw. As smoke forced people to emerge, they were shot. The book places this episode at the end of October 1943 and says 12 to 15 Jews were hiding there.

A second bunker was discovered in early March 1944, only weeks before liberation. The narrative attributes the discovery to local informants and says policemen forced smoke into the shelter with burning straw. Some occupants came out and were shot; those who remained inside burned. The book’s account identifies survivor Shulem Greenberg as the narrator’s source for this episode. Separately, it remembers survivors [Benzion Kleinman](/communities/skala/records/mention_663bdca248aa4ef33972a6ca) and [Menie Shapira](/communities/skala/records/mention_5d486ba56dd4f095d577f7dd), who later recounted a bunker tragedy. The supplied records do not establish that their testimony describes precisely the same bunker or incident as Greenberg’s account.

There is also a numerical discrepancy worth preserving. One memorial-book passage says 21 people were burned alive at a hiding place in the forest on March 1, 1944. The account of the second bunker describes the attack as early in March, while the book’s appended crime list specifies March 1 and gives 21 deaths. Those details may refer to the same massacre, but the text does not warrant a more exact reconciliation of every witness’s account. The list says the crime was investigated and verified by eyewitness testimony; a separate entry reports the forester Czepesiuk was sentenced to death for the crime. These are claims made by the memorial book’s postwar record, not independent confirmation presented here.

The book also recalls survivors finding victims’ bodies and burying them among young pine trees. Its brief record does not name those who performed the burial. The unnamed dead and unnamed survivors are part of the story too: a memorial book can preserve acts and fragments while leaving individual identities unrecoverable.

## What the wider record adds—and what remains open

The broader historical frame helps explain why hiding places were so perilous, without independently verifying each Skala testimony. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum describes the Holocaust in Ukraine as a process of persecution and murder by Nazi Germany and its allies and collaborators, and documents how German forces and local auxiliaries carried out mass shootings across occupied Soviet territory. That regional context is consistent with the violence described in the Skala memorial book, but it is not direct corroboration of the specific bunker episodes. ([USHMM, “The Holocaust and World War II in Ukraine”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/project/the-holocaust-and-world-war-ii-in-ukraine); [USHMM, “Einsatzgruppen massacre sites in Ukraine and surrounding areas”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/map/einsatzgruppen-activity-in-ukraine-and-surrounding-areas).)

Skala-Podilska’s modern history summary notes that most of the town’s Jews perished during the Holocaust in the Borshchiv ghetto. That broad statement underlines why the forest survivors’ story belongs to both Skala and the neighboring communities from which people fled; it does not supply independent evidence about Gatesfeld’s group or its shelters. ([Skala-Podilska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skala-Podilska).) The available independent sources found for this article add regional context, but do not independently verify the named Skala bunker witnesses, the construction details, or the conflicting figures.

The memorial book preserves a community memory of skill, mutual dependence, and terror: shelters built by hand, movement between hiding places, hunger that drove people into danger, songs sung underground, and the smoke that forced people into the open. Further research could clarify [Chaim Gatesfeld’s family and postwar life](research:Chaim Gatesfeld family and postwar records), the identities of the six winter bunker builders, the separate accounts of the second bunker, and the archival documentation of the March 1944 investigation and trial.
